planting.note: Plant nursery-grown container specimens in fall into consistently moist, strongly acidic, peaty soil in partial shade, replicating the sphagnum bogs and boreal peatlands where this evergreen shrub naturally grows.

directions: Plant nursery-grown container specimens in fall into consistently moist, strongly acidic, peaty soil in partial shade, replicating the sphagnum bogs and boreal peatlands of the Great Lakes region and points north where this evergreen ericaceous shrub naturally grows. Clusters of small white flowers open in late spring and are visited by bees and flies, while the dense, leathery, rust-fuzzed foliage provides year-round cover for birds along bog and wetland edges. Leaves are aromatic and were historically brewed as tea, though they contain compounds that are toxic to livestock if browsed in quantity, so this is a plant for wildlife habitat and ornamental bog gardens rather than for foraging. Best suited to a dedicated acidic bog garden alongside pitcher plants, sundews, and cranberry rather than average garden soil.

planting.note: Sow seed directly into saturated, organic-rich soil in fall so winter cold naturally breaks dormancy, or transplant rooted stem sections into a bog garden or pond margin in spring.

directions: Sow seed directly into saturated, organic-rich soil in fall so winter cold naturally breaks dormancy, or transplant rooted stem sections into a bog garden or pond margin in spring. This sprawling, semi-woody perennial produces unusually dark maroon-red, star-shaped flowers through summer that stand out against its blue-green, strawberry-like foliage and attract bees, flies, and other pollinators drawn to its unusual color and scent. It roots at the nodes as it spreads across floating mats and quaking bog edges, helping stabilize soft wetland substrates and providing cover for amphibians and aquatic invertebrates. Found in fens, bogs, and pond margins across the Great Lakes and northern Appalachians, it thrives in permanently saturated, acidic to neutral soil in partial sun.

planting.note: Plant only nursery-propagated, tissue-cultured specimens in fall into consistently moist, neutral to alkaline, calcium-rich soil in partial shade; never dig from the wild, and expect slow establishment but a long-lived clump once sited correctly.

directions: Plant only nursery-propagated, tissue-cultured specimens in fall into consistently moist, neutral to alkaline, calcium-rich soil in partial shade, replicating the calcareous fens and prairie wet meadows of the Great Lakes and upper Midwest where this, the smallest native lady's slipper, naturally occurs. Its compact white pouches with twisted, maroon-striped lateral petals bloom in late spring and are pollinated by small bees that enter seeking non-existent nectar and exit dusted with pollen. Populations have declined sharply with fen and prairie wetland loss, so it is state-listed as rare or threatened across much of its range; never dig from the wild, and expect a slow-establishing but long-lived clump once sited correctly. A rewarding specialty plant for a constructed calcareous seep or fen garden rather than average acidic woodland soil.

planting.note: Surface-sow seed onto consistently moist, calcium-rich, neutral to alkaline soil in fall so winter cold and moisture trigger germination the following spring; seed needs light and should not be buried.

directions: Surface-sow seed onto consistently moist, calcium-rich, neutral to alkaline soil in fall so winter cold and moisture trigger germination the following spring, since seed needs light and should not be buried. Despite its common name it is not a grass at all but a low perennial forb, producing single, five-petaled, cream-white flowers etched with delicate green veining atop wiry stems in late summer and fall — a period when few other wetland natives are still blooming. This late-season nectar makes it valuable for bees, flies, and other pollinators stocking up before winter, and it is a signature species of calcareous fens and wet, sedge-dominated meadows across the Appalachian and Great Lakes region. Site it in a permanently damp, mineral-rich seep or fen garden for best results.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings directly in shallow water or moist mud, then transplant in spring along pond edges, marsh margins, or shallow standing water.

directions: Root stem cuttings directly in shallow water or moist mud, then transplant in spring along pond edges, marsh margins, or shallow standing water where this arching, semi-woody wetland shrub naturally forms dense colonies. Where its long stems arch over and touch water they root at the tip, gradually building thickets that stabilize soft shorelines and create rich cover and spawning habitat for fish, amphibians, and waterfowl. Showy magenta-pink flower clusters bloom in the leaf axils through summer and draw bees and other pollinators, while the tangled root mass filters runoff and reduces erosion along pond and marsh edges throughout the eastern US and Great Lakes basin. Give it full sun to partial shade and a spot that stays wet or seasonally flooded for best colonization.

planting.note: Surface-sow seed onto saturated, nutrient-poor, acidic peat or sand in fall, leaving seed uncovered since it needs light plus winter cold to germinate the following season.

directions: Surface-sow seed onto saturated, nutrient-poor, acidic peat or sand in fall, leaving seed uncovered since it needs light plus winter cold to germinate the following season. This small, wiry, tufted sedge produces distinctive bristly white beaked spikelets in summer that stand out against the dark peat of bogs and poor fens, and its abundant seed is foraged by waterfowl and sparrows through fall and winter. It is a characteristic, low-competition component of acidic bog and fen plant communities across the Great Lakes and Appalachian highlands, helping fill in bare peat and stabilize saturated substrates alongside sundews and pitcher plants. Best used in a constructed bog garden or wetland restoration planting rather than conventional garden soil.

planting.note: Direct sow into calcareous, sandy to gravelly soil in fall so winter moisture and cold stratify the seed naturally; source seed or plants only from reputable native nurseries or restoration programs, since this Great Lakes endemic is federally threatened.

directions: Direct sow into calcareous, sandy to gravelly soil in fall so winter moisture and cold stratify the seed naturally, matching the interdunal wetlands and wet, calcium-rich shoreline swales of the Great Lakes where this goldenrod is endemic and found nowhere else in the world. It tolerates the fluctuating wet-to-dry conditions typical of dune swale habitat once established, and its late-summer to fall clusters of small golden flower heads are an important nectar and pollen source for native bees, migrating monarchs, and other pollinators fueling up before winter or migration. Because it is federally listed as threatened, source seed or plants only from reputable native nurseries or restoration programs rather than wild populations. A valuable, regionally distinctive choice for shoreline restoration or a sunny, sandy, moisture-retentive native planting in Michigan, Wisconsin, and the Ontario Great Lakes shoreline.
